steps.title: Set up the block
steps.instruction: Put the immersion heater and the thermometer into the 1.0 kg aluminium block, with a drop of oil in the thermometer hole. Wrap the block in insulation.

steps.title: Start temperature, then heat
steps.instruction: Record the starting temperature, then switch the heater on and start timing.

steps.title: Read the meters
steps.instruction: With the heater on, read the voltmeter (across the heater) and the ammeter (in series with it) and record both.

steps.title: A reading every minute
steps.instruction: Every minute for 10 minutes, read the thermometer and record the temperature.

steps.title: Switch off at 10 minutes
steps.instruction: Switch the heater off after exactly 10 minutes. Leave the hot block alone: it stays hot for a long time.

steps.title: Energy supplied
steps.instruction: Work out the energy supplied, E = V × I × t, and enter it in joules.

steps.title: Find c
steps.instruction: Use E = m c Δθ to work out the specific heat capacity of aluminium and enter it.

set-1.text: Heat must go into the block, and the thermometer must feel the block quickly.

set-2.text: Put the heater and the thermometer in their holes, add a drop of oil to the thermometer hole, then wrap the block in insulation.

set-3.text: Use the four set-up switches: heater in, thermometer in, oil, insulation.

met-1.text: Power = voltage × current. You need both.

met-2.text: The voltmeter is across the heater; the ammeter is in series with it. Read each one.

met-3.text: Type 11.8 V and 4.10 A and record them while the heater is on.

start-1.text: You need the temperature before any heating starts.

start-2.text: Read the thermometer first, then switch the heater on.

read-1.text: One reading every minute, for ten minutes.

read-2.text: Press "Wait 1 min", then read the thermometer and record it.

read-3.text: Repeat wait-then-record until you reach 10 minutes.

off-1.text: The heating time must be exactly what you use in E = VIt.

off-2.text: Switch the heater off at 10 minutes.

off-3.text: Press Heater off once the clock shows 10:00.

en-2.text: E = V × I × t, with t in seconds.

c-1.text: E = m c Δθ, so c = E ÷ (m Δθ).

c-2.text: Δθ = final temperature − starting temperature; m = 1.0 kg.

c-3.text: With your readings c is about 29 028 ÷ 30.7 ≈ 946 J/kg°C.

observations.whatHappened: The temperature of the block rose steadily, about 3 °C every minute, from 20.0 °C to about 50.7 °C in 10 minutes. The value of c came out at about 946 J/kg°C, a little above the textbook value of 900 J/kg°C.
observations.why: The heater turns electrical energy into thermal energy at a rate P = VI. All of it should go into the block: E = m c Δθ. Some energy still escapes to the air through the insulation, and the thermometer lags slightly behind the block, so the measured Δθ is a bit too small and the calculated c a bit too big. Insulation and the drop of oil make both errors smaller.

prompts.question: Your value of c is higher than the true value. The most likely reason is…
choices: Some energy was lost to the surroundings
prompts.explain: Energy lost to the air did not heat the block, so Δθ was smaller than it should be and c = E/(mΔθ) came out too big.

prompts.question: Why put a drop of oil in the thermometer hole?
choices: To make good thermal contact so the thermometer reads the block temperature
prompts.explain: Air is a poor conductor. Oil fills the gap so heat reaches the thermometer quickly.

prompts.question: Water has c = 4200 J/kg°C, aluminium about 900 J/kg°C. With the same heater and mass, which warms faster?
choices: They warm at the same rate
prompts.explain: Aluminium needs less energy per kilogram per degree, so the same power raises its temperature more quickly.

captions.text: A 1 kg aluminium block. The heater goes in one hole and the thermometer in the other, with a drop of oil for good contact.
Insulation keeps heat in the block instead of escaping to the room.
Start temperature first, then switch on and start the clock.
Power = voltage × current: 11.8 V × 4.10 A ≈ 48 W, so 48 joules every second.
Every minute the block warms by about 3 °C. A steady rise means steady power.
After 600 s: E = VIt ≈ 29 000 J went into the block.
c = E ÷ (m Δθ) ≈ 946 J/kg°C. A bit above 900 because some heat still escaped.
